newsitem.title: USA: Christopher has full agenda on Africa trip.
newsitem.headline: Christopher has full agenda on Africa trip.

text.p: Secretary of State Warren Christopher, on his first trip to sub-Saharan Africa next month, will stress U.S. support for democracy, African solutions to African problems and the need for increased trade, not aid, U.S. officials said on Tuesday.
Christopher will leave Washington on October 7 and make stops in Mali, Ethiopia, Tanzania, Angola and South Africa before returning October 15, spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

The secretary "will underscore during this trip the firm commitment of the United States to help further democracy and economic development and trade, regional integration and conflict resolution on the African continent," Burns said.
"We have broad interests there. And I think we've conveyed a sense of interest and commitment to improving our relations with African countries," he added.

Vice President Al Gore, National Security Adviser Anthony Lake -- an Africa expert -- Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott and George Moose, the assistant secretary of state for African affairs, all have travelled in sub-Saharan Africa.

But during more than three years in office, Christopher has confined his African stops to Egypt and other countries in the northern sector of the continent. He has made more than 18 trips to the Middle East.

Officials said Christopher had long wanted to visit sub-Saharan Africa. He finally made the decision to do so at least in part because he feels "he hasn't paid sufficient attention to the developing world," one official told Reuters.
"He knows there's a movement of great change in Africa and he wants to visibly demonstrate he's not an Africa-pessimist and that we shouldn't write it (Africa) off," the official said.

Some officials said the trip's timing had a political calculation. It takes place a month before the presidential election and hence is likely to be viewed favourably by African-American voters and reflect well on President Bill Clinton.
Christopher's first stop will be Bamako, Mali, where he will meet President Alpha Oumar Konare and other officials.
"Mali has made some very important steps toward democracy and toward representative government. And the secretary felt it was important to mark that and to give encouragement to it," Burns said.

The next stop will be Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, where Christopher will meet Prime Minister Meles Zenawi to discuss bilateral issues and regional issues. He will also meet the chairman of the Organisation of African Unity to discuss how the United States can best support some of the conflict resolution efforts the OAU has taken a lead on.

The secretary then goes to Arusha, Tanzania, for talks with President Benjamin Mkapa and former president Julius Nyerere. He will also meet other leaders from Central and East Africa on economic integration and development issues.
Christopher will use the Tanzania stop to talk about the problems in nearby Burundi and the Rwanda war crimes tribunal, Burns said.

He will spend several hours in Luanda, Angola, meeting President Jose Eduardo dos Santos and UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi, a former strong U.S. ally. Dos Santos and Savimbi formed a unity government after ending their decades-long war.
The visit "is meant to stimulate further movement toward full national reconciliation in Angola," Burns said.
The final stop is Cape Town, South Africa, where Christopher will meet President Nelson Mandela, Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, Archbishop Desmond Tutu and other leaders.

"Because of the extraordinary changes there and because of the very close relationship the Clinton administration has had with President Mandela, the secretary felt it was important to continue those and continue to deepen that relationship," Burns said.

Christopher is not, however, visiting three of the most important countries in Africa -- Nigeria, Zaire and Kenya -- because of U.S. problems with the lack of progress in those countries toward democracy and human rights, officials said.
